overview: Two outcomes of introducing foreign DNA into cultured cells, distinguished by whether the DNA integrates and persists across generations.
genZNote: Stable transfection moves in permanently. Transient transfection is just crashing on the couch for a few days.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Foreign DNA integrates into the host genome, allowing long-term, heritable expression across cell divisions.
aspects.valueB: Foreign DNA remains episomal (non-integrated) and is diluted out or degraded over subsequent cell divisions.

aspects.label: Duration of Expression
aspects.valueA: Long-term, persistent expression, often for the life of the cell line.
aspects.valueB: Short-term, typically peaking within 24-72 hours and declining thereafter.

aspects.label: Selection Requirement
aspects.valueA: Requires a selectable marker (e.g. antibiotic resistance gene) and a selection period to isolate stably transfected clones.
aspects.valueB: No selection needed — cells are simply assayed shortly after transfection.

aspects.label: Time and Cost
aspects.valueA: Time-consuming (weeks) and more labor-intensive to establish a stable cell line.
aspects.valueB: Fast and relatively inexpensive, suitable for quick functional assays.

aspects.label: Applications
aspects.valueA: Generating stable cell lines for long-term protein production or reporter assays.
aspects.valueB: Rapid protein expression testing, promoter/reporter assays, and short-term overexpression or knockdown studies.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: DNA integrates; long-lasting expression requiring selection.
aspects.valueB: DNA stays episomal; short-lived expression, no selection needed.
